Anthropic says Claude Mythos 5 designed quantum circuits that beat the best published designs on eight tasks.
One new design needs 17 times fewer gates, and a decoder circuit got 12 times cheaper than Google's version.
The savings are estimates for future quantum computers, not today's machines.

slides.headline: Claude just beat the best published quantum circuit designs, one with *17 times fewer gates*

slides.heading: Claude *drew the blueprints*
paras: Anthropic says Claude Mythos 5 improved on the best published quantum circuits for eight building blocks, from chemistry and optimization to physics simulation and number theory.
Some gains were an order of magnitude or more. In seven of the eight tasks, the new circuits cut both gate and qubit counts.

slides.heading: 53 hours, *no human in the loop*
paras: Claude wrote each design as a Python program. An automated evaluator checked it for correctness and scored it, and Claude revised with no human input between rounds.
The main run lasted 53 hours from a one-paragraph brief. Researcher Andi Gu led the work, with collaborators from Harvard and QuEra Computing.

slides.heading: The *17x* breakthrough
paras: For elliptic-curve math, Claude found a new way to run modular inversion on a quantum computer without storing the history of its branching steps.
One design uses 12% more qubits but 17 times fewer gates than the smallest previous design. Claude proved the method correct in the Lean proof language.

slides.heading: Beating *Google's* design too
paras: Claude also rebuilt the decoder inside decoded quantum interferometry, a quantum optimization method. Its circuit needs 12 times fewer gates than Google's previous construction.

paras.t: Today's quantum computers have only hundreds to thousands of noisy qubits, so these savings are estimates for future machines.

slides.hook: AI is now designing the computers of the future. Follow to see what Claude cracks next.
